title: TicTacTale
subtitle: Turn-Based Duel · In development
description: An original solo game in Unity 6 that turns tic-tac-toe into a best-of duel between two named fighters. Astraea and Kyra each enter with a pool of lives, every round won drains one from the loser, and the match only ends when a life bar empties — so a single lucky opening no longer decides anything. Currently in development: the full flow from main menu through character matching to the battle scene is playable, and most of the work so far has gone into making a board game feel like it has weight.

mechanics.title: Best-of Lives Duel
mechanics.description: Rather than one board deciding everything, each round won drains a life from the loser, who then starts the next round. A single lucky opening no longer wins the match, and the board resets without a scene reload — turn order, life pools and match-over state all live in one place, surfaced as segmented health bars either side of the board.

mechanics.title: Impact-Frame Placement
mechanics.description: Placing a pawn is a four-stage DOTween sequence: it accelerates down on InCubic so it lands rather than arrives, squashes wide and flat on contact, holds a 40 ms hitstop on the impact frame, then settles on OutBack for a single overshoot. The hitstop is what sells the weight — OutElastic was rejected here because several bounces read bouncy instead of heavy.

mechanics.title: Staggered Win Reveal
mechanics.description: When a line completes, each pawn on it clips shut to zero width, swaps to its win pose while nothing is on screen, and clips back open — staggered along the line so the reveal travels like a blade sweeping through. Only the X axis overshoots on the way out, because bouncing both axes double-bounces off the pinch.

mechanics.title: Cross-Scene Match Handoff
mechanics.description: The matching screen's character picks travel into the battle scene through a static match record instead of a persistent GameObject, with a HasData flag so the battle scene still runs standalone on scene defaults when it is played directly in the editor. Whoever was picked becomes both the portrait beside the board and the token played into every cell.

mechanics.title: Bot Opponent
mechanics.description: A coroutine-driven opponent that waits a randomised beat before moving, so its turn reads as thinking rather than as an instant response. The board is written as a generic N×N grid with row, column and both diagonal win checks, so the 3×3 rule set is a serialised field rather than a hard-coded assumption.

codeHighlights.label: Pawn.cs
codeHighlights.note: The game feel work — strike, squash, hitstop and settle, with the easing choices explained in comments.

codeHighlights.label: BoardManager.cs
codeHighlights.note: Round flow, life pools and N×N win detection — the one place that owns match state.

codeHighlights.label: MatchData.cs
codeHighlights.note: Static match record that carries the matchup across a scene load, with an editor-standalone fallback.

codeHighlights.label: Cell.cs
codeHighlights.note: A cell reports its click and nothing else — the manager decides whether the move is legal.

title: FPS Inventory System
subtitle: Gameplay Prototype
description: A Unity prototype for a first-person shooter inventory and interaction system, including weapon pickup, switching, and UI-based management. Designed with a test-ready gameplay loop and refined through iterative debugging to ensure smooth and responsive player interactions.

mechanics.title: Weapon Pickup & Switching
mechanics.description: Seamless weapon pickup, inventory management, and switching logic with a clean UI-driven experience built for test-ready prototyping.

mechanics.title: UI-Based Management
mechanics.description: A responsive inventory HUD system that visually communicates weapon states, ammo counts, and interaction prompts clearly to the player.

mechanics.title: Player Interaction System
mechanics.description: Raycasting-based interaction system allowing the player to pick up, drop, and cycle weapons with tight, responsive feel tuning.

mechanics.title: Iterative Polish
mechanics.description: Refined through multiple playtest cycles to ensure smooth, bug-free gameplay loops and responsive player feedback at all times.

codeHighlights.label: Inventory.cs
codeHighlights.note: The inventory model itself — holding, swapping and dropping weapons across slots.

codeHighlights.label: Player.cs
codeHighlights.note: Raycast pickup and the interaction entry point that drives everything else.

codeHighlights.label: Gun.cs
codeHighlights.note: Weapon definition and per-weapon state, kept separate from the UI that shows it.

codeHighlights.label: PrimaryGunPanel.cs
codeHighlights.note: Slot panel logic — the largest UI class, handling drag, assign and clear.

title: The Cursed Chaos
subtitle: Horror Game
description: A horror prototype built in Unity 6. You play a software engineer whose mountain-forest getaway turns into something much worse. I built the interaction and inventory systems, the task and objective flow, and the atmosphere-driven level design, then staged the story beats in Timeline. Character movement starts from Unity's Starter Assets controller and the avatars come from Ready Player Me — the gameplay systems layered on top of them are mine.

mechanics.title: Traversal & Interaction
mechanics.description: Movement builds on Unity's Starter Assets controller; the interaction layer on top is mine — raycast examine and pickup on E, and a toggleable flashlight that is the player's only reliable light source.

mechanics.title: Inventory & Resource Management
mechanics.description: A pickup and inventory system where limited supplies have to be rationed across a run, so what the player chooses to carry actually matters.

mechanics.title: Task & Objective System
mechanics.description: A dedicated task system tracks objectives through the run and drives what the player is told to do next, so the level can gate progress on exploration rather than on a linear corridor.

mechanics.title: Timeline-Driven Cutscenes
mechanics.description: Story beats are staged with Unity Timeline and Cinemachine over Ready Player Me avatars, handing camera control between gameplay and cutscene without breaking the player's sense of place.

codeHighlights.label: MainManager.cs
codeHighlights.note: Central game state — run flow, pausing and scene-level coordination.

codeHighlights.label: Task System/
codeHighlights.note: Objective tracking that decides what the player is asked to do next.

codeHighlights.label: Interaction Scripts/
codeHighlights.note: Interactable objects and the contracts they share with the player.

codeHighlights.label: ScriptableObjects/
codeHighlights.note: Data-driven content kept as assets instead of hard-coded values.

title: Kitchen Chaos
subtitle: 3D Cooking Game
description: A 3D kitchen sim where you assemble recipes against a timer — grab ingredients, chop them, fry them, plate them and deliver before the clock runs out, scoring on how many orders you complete. Built by working through Code Monkey's Kitchen Chaos course as a deliberate study in clean Unity architecture: interfaces, ScriptableObject-driven data and event-based communication instead of one script that does everything.

mechanics.title: Polymorphic Counter Hierarchy
mechanics.description: Every station — clear, container, cutting, stove, plates, delivery and trash — derives from a single BaseCounter. Adding a new station means writing one subclass instead of touching the player or any counter that already works.

mechanics.title: Interface-Driven Interaction
mechanics.description: IKitchenObjectParent lets the player, the counters and the plates all hold ingredients through one shared contract, and IHaveProgress drives every progress bar in the game — chopping and frying alike — from the same UI component.

mechanics.title: ScriptableObject-Driven Content
mechanics.description: Ingredients and recipes live as ScriptableObject assets rather than hard-coded values, so the recipe list and cutting or frying timings can be rebalanced in the editor without touching code.

mechanics.title: Event-Driven Game State
mechanics.description: A GameManager runs the countdown state machine while DeliveryManager validates plated orders against the active recipe list. C# events keep visuals and audio subscribed to gameplay rather than wired into it, which is why the visual scripts live in their own layer.

codeHighlights.label: BaseCounter.cs
codeHighlights.note: The base class all seven station types inherit from.

codeHighlights.label: IKitchenObjectParent.cs
codeHighlights.note: One contract that lets player, counters and plates all hold ingredients.

codeHighlights.label: IHaveProgress.cs
codeHighlights.note: Why chopping and frying share a single progress-bar component.

codeHighlights.label: DeliveryManager.cs
codeHighlights.note: Validates a plated order against the active recipe list and scores it.
